item.title: Sounds, Alphabet, and Greetings
item.description: Lesson 1: Sounds, Alphabet, and Greetings German spelling is highly regular, and learning its sounds early prevents years of guessing. The alphabet has 26 letters plus three umlauted vowels — ä, ö, ü — and the letter ß, called Eszett or scharfes S, which sounds like a sharp s and never appears at…

item.title: Sein, Haben, and Describing Yourself
item.description: Lesson 2: Sein, Haben, and Describing Yourself Sein (to be) and haben (to have) are the two most frequent verbs, and both are irregular. Present tense of sein: ich bin, du bist, er/sie/es ist, wir sind, ihr seid, sie/Sie sind. Present tense of haben: ich habe, du hast, er/sie/es hat, wir haben, ihr…

item.title: Regular Verbs and Word Order
item.description: Lesson 3: Regular Verbs and Word Order Regular German verbs in the present tense add endings to the stem, which is the infinitive minus -en (or -n after a vowel). For machen (to make/do), the stem is mach-: ich mache, du machst, er/sie/es macht, wir machen, ihr macht, sie/Sie machen. The pattern…

item.title: Cases — Nominative, Accusative, and Dative
item.description: Lesson 4: Cases — Nominative, Accusative, and Dative German cases show the role of a noun in a sentence, and articles and adjective endings change accordingly. There are four cases; this lesson covers the first three, which carry most everyday conversation. The nominative is the subject: Der Mann…

item.title: The Past Tense — Perfekt
item.description: Lesson 5: The Past Tense — Perfekt Spoken German tells the past mainly with the Perfekt, formed with the present of haben or sein plus the past participle, which usually goes to the end of the clause: Ich habe gelernt (I learned / I have learned), Wir sind gegangen (We went / We have gone). item.title: Future, Modal Verbs, and the Weather
item.description: Lesson 7: Future, Modal Verbs, and the Weather German expresses the future in two main ways.
